subject: history
prompt: In colonies like India, the growth of modern nationalism is closely tied to the **anti-colonial movement** (the struggle against colonial rule). Why?

image.alt: Figures from different groups moving towards a shared struggle

options.text: Colonial rulers deliberately taught Indians to feel like one nation
People discovered their unity while struggling together against colonial rule
Every class and group understood freedom in exactly the same way
Nationalism started only after the colonial rulers had left

hint: Think of what a shared experience of oppression does to different groups.
explanation: In colonies, the sense of being **oppressed under colonialism** gave many different groups a shared bond, so people found their unity in the struggle itself. The unity was not automatic: each class felt colonialism differently and their ideas of freedom were **not always the same**, which is why the Congress had to work to hold the groups together.

subject: history
prompt: During the First World War, **defence expenditure** (spending on the army and war) increased hugely. How did the colonial government pay for it?

image.alt: Flow chart from the war to higher defence spending and doubled prices, with the way it was paid for left as a question

options.text: Through war loans and higher taxes, with customs duties raised and income tax introduced
By cutting customs duties and abolishing income tax to please traders
Through gifts of money from the Ottoman emperor
By fixing prices so that nothing became costlier

hint: The money had to come from borrowing and from people's pockets.
explanation: The war raised defence spending sharply. It was financed by **war loans and increasing taxes**: customs duties were raised and **income tax was introduced**. Prices then **doubled between 1913 and 1918**, so ordinary people suffered. Lower taxes, foreign gifts or price control are the opposite of what happened.

subject: history
prompt: Prices **doubled between 1913 and 1918**. A packet of grain cost ₹6 in 1913. On this basis, how much would it cost in 1918?

image.alt: Bar chart of a price index: 100 in 1913 and 200 in 1918

hint: Doubling means multiplying by 2.
explanation: Doubled means $6 \times 2 = 12$, so **₹12**. Traps: ₹3 halves the price instead of doubling it; ₹8 adds 2 instead of multiplying; ₹18 treats doubling as a rise of 200 per cent (a 200 per cent rise would triple the price).

subject: history
prompt: In 1918-19 and 1920-21, **crops failed** in many parts of India. Food became scarce (hard to get). Tap the part of the scene that shows this.

image.alt: Scene with a price board, a tax desk, a dry field, an official with villagers and a sick person in bed

hint: Look for the withered plants.
explanation: The dry, withered field shows **crop failure**. Together with the influenza epidemic, it caused acute food shortages: the 1921 census said **12 to 13 million people perished** in the famines and the epidemic. The price board, tax desk and recruiting official show the other war-time burdens.

subject: history
prompt: Which of these were hardships faced by Indians during and just after the First World War? Select all that apply.

Income tax was abolished
An influenza epidemic spread

hint: Think of money, army, harvests and health.
explanation: Prices doubled, **forced recruitment** caused anger in villages, crops failed twice and an influenza epidemic added to the suffering. Taxes went **up**: customs duties were raised and income tax was *introduced*, so abolishing income tax or reducing duties is wrong.

subject: history
prompt: What did the idea of **satyagraha** give importance to?

image.alt: A peaceful person appeals to an oppressor's conscience

options.text: Passive resistance, the weapon of the weak
The power of truth and non-violence, appealing to the conscience of the oppressor
Fighting force with force until the oppressor is defeated
Taking revenge on the oppressor after winning

hint: Recall what Gandhiji said a satyagrahi does NOT do.
explanation: Satyagraha stressed **truth and the search for truth**. A satyagrahi fights injustice **without physical force, vengeance or aggression**, persuading even the oppressor to see the truth. Gandhiji said it is *not* passive resistance: it calls for intense activity and can be used only by the strong.

subject: history
prompt: Match each satyagraha of 1917-1919 with the people or cause it involved.

image.alt: Three vignettes: a plantation, a cotton mill and a dry field

Cotton mill workers

Nationwide hartal against an Act allowing detention without trial

hint: Plantation, mill, field, law: one cause for each.
explanation: In **Champaran** (Bihar) Gandhiji inspired peasants against the plantation system; in **Ahmedabad** he organised cotton mill workers; in **Kheda** (Gujarat) peasants hit by crop failure and plague wanted revenue relaxed; in 1919 the **Rowlatt satyagraha** was a nationwide protest.

subject: history
prompt: Which power did the **Rowlatt Act (1919)** give the government?

image.alt: A law scroll beside a jail window, and a court crossed out

options.text: Banning all trade with foreign countries
Taxing salt more heavily
Closing every school run by Indians
Detaining political prisoners without trial for two years

hint: The Act was about repressing political activity.
explanation: The Rowlatt Act was passed in a hurry despite united opposition from Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council. It gave the government **enormous powers to repress political activities** and allowed **detention without trial for two years**. The salt tax and school boycotts belong to other chapters of the story.

subject: history

Gandhiji calls off the movement as violence spreads

explanation: The hartal was on **6 April**; after the police fired in Amritsar on **10 April**, attacks followed, martial law was imposed and Dyer took command; the **Jallianwalla Bagh** incident came on **13 April**. Seeing violence spread, Gandhiji **called off** the movement.

subject: history
prompt: On 13 April 1919, General Dyer entered the enclosed ground (ground with walls around it). He **blocked the exit points** and then opened fire. Tap the part of the ground that he blocked.

image.alt: Enclosed ground with brick walls, a fair stall, a crowd, a narrow gateway and a notice board

hint: Which part lets people leave the ground?
explanation: The ground was **enclosed**, so blocking the exit points left the crowd with no way out. Dyer later said his object was to **produce a moral effect**, creating terror and awe in the minds of satyagrahis. Many villagers at the Baisakhi fair were unaware that martial law had been imposed.

subject: history
prompt: Why did Gandhiji take up the **Khilafat** issue in 1919-20?

image.alt: Two groups of people joined by a bridge with clasped hands, labelled Khilafat issue

options.text: He saw it as a chance to bring Hindus and Muslims together in one broad-based national movement
He wanted Congress to support the Ottoman emperor's army
He wanted to end the Rowlatt Act through the Khilafat Committee
He wanted Muslims to leave the Congress

hint: Gandhiji felt a mass movement needed Hindu-Muslim unity.
explanation: The Rowlatt satyagraha was mostly in cities and towns. Gandhiji felt a **broader movement** needed Hindus and Muslims closer, and the Khilafat issue (the fear of a harsh treaty for the Ottoman emperor, the Khalifa) offered a way to bring **Muslims under a unified national movement**. The Calcutta session (September 1920) agreed on non-cooperation for Khilafat and swaraj.

subject: history
prompt: In *Hind Swaraj* (1909), Gandhiji explained why British rule in India survived. According to him, what did it survive because of?

image.alt: A heavy block called British rule held up by many people

options.text: The superior arms of the British army alone
The votes of Indians in the legislative councils
The cooperation of Indians; without it British rule would collapse
The goodwill of the Ottoman emperor

hint: If a block stands on people's shoulders, what happens when they step away?
explanation: Gandhiji declared that British rule had been established with the **cooperation of Indians** and survived only because of it. If Indians **refused to cooperate**, rule would collapse within a year and swaraj would come. This is the idea behind the Non-Cooperation Movement.

subject: history
prompt: Arrange these events in chronological order (the order in which they happened).

Calcutta session of the Congress backs non-cooperation

hint: The Congress had to agree on the programme before the movement could begin.
explanation: The Khilafat Committee (March 1919) came first. At **Calcutta (September 1920)** Gandhiji convinced the Congress; after a tussle a compromise at **Nagpur (December 1920)** adopted the programme. The movement began in **January 1921** and ended after **Chauri Chaura in February 1922**.

subject: history
prompt: Gandhiji proposed that non-cooperation should **unfold in stages** (happen step by step). Arrange these steps in the order he proposed.

items.text: The government responds with repression

A full civil disobedience campaign is launched
Boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, councils, schools and foreign goods

hint: Civil disobedience was held back for the case of repression.
explanation: The movement was to begin with **surrender of titles** and a **boycott** of institutions and foreign goods. **Only if** the government used repression would a **full civil disobedience campaign** be launched.

subject: history
prompt: In 1921, foreign cloth worth ₹102 crore was imported. In 1922, this fell to ₹57 crore. By how many crore rupees did it fall?

image.alt: Bar chart of foreign cloth imports: 102 crore rupees in 1921, 57 crore rupees in 1922

options.text: ₹159 crore
₹45 crore
₹51 crore
₹57 crore

explanation: The fall is $102 - 57 = 45$, so **₹45 crore** (a drop of about 44%, which is why the text says imports *roughly halved*). Traps: ₹159 crore adds the two years; ₹51 crore is exactly half of 102, which confuses 'roughly halved' with an exact figure; ₹57 crore is the later value, not the difference.

subject: history
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

subject: history
prompt: In the early 1920s, the hill people of the **Gudem Hills** became very angry. What made them angry?

image.alt: A forest behind a closed barrier, with a cow and a villager left outside

explanation: The colonial government **closed large forest areas**, so people could not graze cattle or collect fuelwood and fruits, and then forced them to contribute **begar** for roads. Their guerrilla movement was led by Alluri Sitaram Raju, who thought India could be freed only by force. Landlords' rents describe Awadh; the Inland Emigration Act describes Assam plantations.

subject: history
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Tea garden behind a fence, a train and village huts

explanation: In February 1922 Gandhiji **withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement**, feeling it was turning violent and that satyagrahis needed proper training before mass struggles. The Civil Disobedience Movement began much later, in 1930, with the salt march.

subject: history
prompt: Arrange these developments in the order in which they happened.

subject: history
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A scroll with the words Purna Swaraj and a crowd below

explanation: Both are true and R explains A. The Lahore Congress declared that 26 January 1930 would be celebrated as Independence Day, but the celebrations **attracted very little attention**. *So* Gandhiji had to relate this **abstract idea of freedom** to concrete issues of everyday life, and he found such an issue in **salt**.

subject: history
prompt: Gandhiji found **salt** a powerful symbol to unite the nation. Why?

image.alt: A heap of salt with people on both sides and a coin above

options.text: Only the rich consumed it, so taxing it hurt the poor less
Salt was made only in Gandhiji's ashram
Rich and poor alike consumed it, and the tax and government monopoly showed the most oppressive face of British rule
The salt tax was the only demand in his letter to Irwin

hint: A symbol must touch everybody's life.
explanation: Salt was **one of the most essential items of food**, used by the rich and the poor. The **tax on salt and the government monopoly** over production revealed the oppressive face of British rule. His 31 January 1930 letter to Viceroy Irwin had **eleven demands** (not just salt), so all classes could identify with it; the salt-tax demand was the most stirring.

24 miles

image.alt: Scene with an ashram, a line of volunteers, villagers on a bank, the sea and a heap of salt

explanation: The march started from Gandhiji's **ashram at Sabarmati** and ended at the Gujarati coastal town of **Dandi**. On 6 April he reached Dandi and ceremonially broke the law by **making salt from boiling sea water**.

subject: history
prompt: Which statements about the salt march and its background are correct? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A distance line from Sabarmati to Dandi

The march went from Sabarmati ashram to Dandi
At Dandi on 6 April he made salt by boiling sea water
The march began from Delhi
Irwin agreed to abolish the salt tax before the march

explanation: The letter, the **78 volunteers**, the route **Sabarmati to Dandi** and the salt-making on **6 April** are all in the chapter. The march did **not** start from Delhi, and **Irwin was unwilling to negotiate**, which is why Gandhiji began the march after the 11 March deadline in the letter passed.

subject: history
prompt: In the **Civil Disobedience Movement**, people were asked not only to refuse cooperation. They were also asked to **break colonial laws**. Which picture shows breaking a colonial law?

options.text: Making salt from sea water

options.text: Leaving a court

image.alt: A lawyer leaving court

options.text: Giving up a title

image.alt: Giving up a government title

hint: Which act defies a law, rather than just refusing to cooperate?
explanation: Making salt violated the **salt law**, so it is civil disobedience. Leaving schools and courts and surrendering titles were forms of **non-cooperation** in 1921-22: refusing to take part, not breaking a law.

subject: history
prompt: Which of these happened as the **Civil Disobedience Movement** spread? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A heap of salt, a pile of foreign cloth and a picketed liquor shop

options.text: People broke the salt law and manufactured salt
Foreign cloth was boycotted and liquor shops picketed
Peasants refused to pay revenue and chaukidari taxes
Forest people entered Reserved Forests to collect wood and graze cattle
A guerrilla war was fought in the Gudem Hills
A hartal was held against the Rowlatt Act

hint: Two options belong to earlier movements.
explanation: The first four describe the Civil Disobedience Movement of 1930. The **Gudem Hills guerrilla struggle** belonged to the early 1920s, and the **Rowlatt hartal** was in April 1919.

subject: history
prompt: Arrange these events of the Civil Disobedience Movement in order.

image.alt: Timeline of the Civil Disobedience years with icons

items.text: Gandhi-Irwin Pact
Gandhiji sends Irwin a letter with eleven demands
Gandhiji goes to London for the Round Table Conference
Civil Disobedience is relaunched
Gandhiji breaks the salt law at Dandi

hint: Think of how the movement began, paused for talks, and then restarted.
explanation: Gandhiji sent Irwin the letter with eleven demands on **31 January 1930** and broke the salt law at Dandi on **6 April 1930**. Arrests followed and he ended the movement through the **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931)**, agreeing to attend the conference. In **December 1931** talks in London broke down; seeing a new cycle of repression, he **relaunched** the movement in **1932**, which lost momentum by 1934.

subject: history
prompt: Match each place or group with what happened during the Civil Disobedience Movement.

image.alt: Tiles showing a police post, a mill, cotton, a worker, cloth and a sack

right.text: Crowds demonstrated after Abdul Ghaffar Khan's arrest, facing armoured cars and police firing

Thousands of workers wore Gandhi caps in rallies and boycott campaigns
Rich peasants hit hard by falling prices of commercial crops

hint: Match each to the group's action or situation.
explanation: In **Peshawar** angry crowds met armoured cars after Abdul Ghaffar Khan's arrest (April 1930); in **Sholapur** workers attacked symbols of British rule after Gandhiji's arrest; in **Chotanagpur** tin miners wore Gandhi caps; **Patidars and Jats** were rich peasants producing commercial crops.

subject: history
prompt: Rich peasants like the **Patidars and Jats** supported the Civil Disobedience Movement with great enthusiasm. Why?

image.alt: Cotton plants and a sack beside a price line

options.text: They wanted unpaid rent to landlords to be remitted
As producers of commercial crops hit by falling prices, they could not pay the revenue and saw swaraj as a fight against high revenue
They wanted protection from imports and a favourable rupee-sterling ratio
They wanted separate electorates for their community

hint: Think of cash income disappearing during the depression.
explanation: Rich peasants grew **commercial crops**; the **trade depression** destroyed their cash incomes while the government refused to reduce revenue. For them swaraj meant a struggle against **high revenues**. Remission of rent was the demand of small tenants, protection from imports that of business classes. They were disappointed when the movement ended in 1931 with no revenue revision, so many stayed out in 1932.

subject: history
prompt: Many **small tenants** cultivated land rented from landlords. They wanted the **unpaid rent remitted** (cancelled). Tap the small tenant in this picture.

image.alt: Six vignettes of a rich peasant, a tenant, a merchant, a worker, a woman and a student

hint: Look for someone with a spade and a small hut.
explanation: **Small tenants** found it hard to pay rent as the depression cut cash incomes. They joined radical movements, often led by Socialists and Communists, because the Congress was unwilling to support **'no rent' campaigns** in most places. The relationship between poor peasants and the Congress stayed uncertain.

subject: history
prompt: In 1927, industrialists formed the **FICCI** to organise business interests. Tap the group that formed it.

image.alt: Six vignettes of a rich peasant, a tenant, a merchant, a worker, a woman and a student

hint: Which group has a ledger and money?
explanation: **Merchants and industrialists** formed the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress (1920) and the **FICCI (1927)**, led by Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G. D. Birla. They wanted protection against imports and a rupee-sterling ratio that discouraged imports, and gave financial help to the movement.

subject: history
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A mill, a ledger with coins and a crate of imported goods crossed out

assertion: Industrialists supported the Civil Disobedience Movement when it was first launched.
reason: They formed the Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries (FICCI) in 1927.
hint: Does forming FICCI explain WHY they backed the movement?
explanation: Both are true, but R **does not explain** A. Industrialists supported the movement because they **attacked colonial control over the economy** and wanted restrictions on business removed. FICCI was just the body that organised them. After the failure of the Round Table Conference their enthusiasm weakened because of fear of militant activities and socialism.

subject: history
prompt: Which statement about **women in the Civil Disobedience Movement** is correct?

image.alt: A procession of women carrying placards

options.text: They were given positions of authority in the Congress as soon as the movement began
Gandhiji urged them to give up household duties for politics
Thousands joined marches, made salt and picketed shops, yet the Congress was keen only on their symbolic presence
Only women from poor tenant families took part

hint: Public role did not mean a radical change in how women's position was seen.
explanation: Women came out in **large numbers**, manufacturing salt, joining protest marches and picketing foreign cloth and liquor shops; many went to jail. But this did not change how their position was visualised: Gandhiji felt their duty was **home and hearth**, and for long the Congress was reluctant to give them authority. In towns they came from high-caste families, in villages from rich peasant households.

subject: history
prompt: What did the **Poona Pact (September 1932)** provide?

image.alt: A legislative chamber with rows of chairs, some reserved in orange

options.text: Separate electorates for the Depressed Classes
Abolition of all reserved seats for dalits
Reserved seats chosen only by Depressed Class voters
Reserved seats for the Depressed Classes in provincial and central legislative councils, voted in by the general electorate

hint: Ambedkar ultimately accepted Gandhiji's position.
explanation: Ambedkar demanded separate electorates at the second Round Table Conference; when the British conceded it, Gandhiji began a **fast unto death**. The compromise, the **Poona Pact**, gave the Depressed Classes (later Scheduled Castes) **reserved seats** in legislative councils but they were to be **voted in by the general electorate**.

subject: history
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A legislative chamber with rows of chairs

assertion: The Poona Pact gave the Depressed Classes separate electorates.
reason: Gandhiji began a fast unto death against separate electorates for dalits.
hint: Under the Pact, who voted for the reserved seats?
explanation: A is **false**: the Pact gave **reserved seats chosen by the general electorate**, not separate electorates. R is true: Gandhiji believed separate electorates would slow the integration of dalits into society, and the fast pushed Ambedkar to accept the compromise.

subject: history
prompt: In 1927, it seemed possible that the Congress and the Muslim League could work together. **Muhammad Ali Jinnah** was willing to give up the demand for separate electorates on certain terms. What were these terms?

image.alt: Two people on either side of a table with a paper between them

options.text: Dropping the Rowlatt Act and the salt tax
Reserved seats for Muslims in the Central Assembly and representation in proportion to population in Bengal and Punjab
A separate country for Muslims within one year
Removal of all reserved seats from provincial councils

hint: The issue was representation in future assemblies.
explanation: Jinnah was willing to give up separate electorates if Muslims were assured **reserved seats in the Central Assembly** and **proportional representation in the Muslim-majority provinces of Bengal and Punjab**. Hope disappeared at the **All Parties Conference in 1928** when M. R. Jayakar of the Hindu Mahasabha opposed compromise. In 1930 Iqbal defended separate electorates as a safeguard for minority political interests.

subject: history
prompt: By 1921, Gandhiji had designed the **Swaraj flag**. Which item in its centre stood for the Gandhian ideal of **self-help**?

image.alt: A book, a scroll and a spinning wheel as symbols of how nationalism spread through culture

options.text: Lotus

image.alt: A lotus

options.text: Crescent moon

image.alt: A crescent moon

options.text: Spinning wheel

image.alt: A spinning wheel

options.text: Plough

image.alt: A plough

hint: Think of khadi and spinning.
explanation: The 1921 Swaraj flag was a tricolour of red, green and white with a **spinning wheel** in the centre, representing **self-help**. The earlier Swadeshi-movement flag in Bengal had **eight lotuses** (eight provinces of British India) and a **crescent moon** (Hindus and Muslims). Carrying the flag aloft in marches became a symbol of defiance.

subject: history
prompt: In the late nineteenth century, nationalists began **recording folk tales** sung by bards (folk singers). They toured villages to gather folk songs. Tap the person gathering the tales.

image.alt: Village gathering with a singer, a collector with a notebook, listeners, books and a framed print

hint: Look for the one carrying a notebook.
explanation: Nationalists believed folk tales gave a true picture of traditional culture that outside forces had corrupted. Preserving them would help discover **national identity** and restore pride. In Bengal Rabindranath Tagore collected ballads, nursery rhymes and myths; in Madras Natesa Sastri published *The Folklore of Southern India*.

subject: history
prompt: Match each person with the contribution described in the chapter.

image.alt: Tiles showing books, a singer, a spinning wheel, a scroll and a lotus

right.text: Painted the famous image of Bharat Mata
Wrote 'Vande Mataram', later part of Anandamath
Published a four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales
Collected ballads, nursery rhymes and myths in Bengal

hint: Hymn, painting, Bengal folklore, Tamil folklore.
explanation: **Bankim Chandra** wrote *Vande Mataram* in the 1870s and included it in *Anandamath*; **Abanindranath Tagore** painted Bharat Mata in 1905; **Rabindranath Tagore** led the folk revival in Bengal; **Natesa Sastri** published the four-volume *The Folklore of Southern India*.

prompt: Match each term from the chapter with its meaning.

image.alt: Tiles showing a sack, shops, a recruit and a train

right.text: Refusal to deal with people, take part in activities or use things, as a protest
Labour villagers were forced to give without payment

hint: Match the word to the definition in the 'New words' boxes.
explanation: **Begar** is unpaid forced labour; a **boycott** is refusing to deal or participate; a **picket** blocks an entrance; **forced recruitment** is compelling people to join the army.

subject: history
prompt: Which statements about the **Hindustan Socialist Republican Army (HSRA)** are correct? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A newspaper dated 1928 and a megaphone

options.text: It was founded in 1928 at Ferozeshah Kotla ground in Delhi
Bhagat Singh and Batukeswar Dutta threw a bomb in the Legislative Assembly in April 1929
Bhagat Singh said he did not wish to glorify 'the cult of the bomb and pistol' but wanted a revolution in society
It was formed by C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru to enter the councils
It supported Gandhiji's non-violent methods

hint: These nationalists doubted that non-violence could win.
explanation: The HSRA was formed in **1928** by nationalists who thought non-violence could not win. It targeted symbols of British power, such as the bomb in the Legislative Assembly (**April 1929**). Das and Nehru formed the **Swaraj Party**, not the HSRA.

subject: history
prompt: Which statements about the **Quit India Movement** are correct? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A procession with placards while shops stay shut

options.text: The Congress Working Committee passed the 'Quit India' resolution at Wardha on 14 July 1942
The All India Congress Committee endorsed it in Bombay on 8 August 1942, when Gandhiji gave the 'Do or Die' speech
Students, workers and peasants took part, along with leaders and women such as Matangini Hazra
It was launched after the first Round Table Conference
The British put it down within a few weeks

hint: It followed the failure of the Cripps Mission.
explanation: The movement demanded immediate transfer of power and the withdrawal of the British. It was a non-violent mass struggle with hartals, processions and national songs. The British responded with force, but it took **more than a year** to suppress it.

subject: history
prompt: The spinning wheel in the centre of the 1921 Swaraj flag stood for Gandhian **self-help**. Tap the spinning wheel in this scene.

image.alt: Boycott scene with a school, a court, a spinning wheel, a bonfire and people at a liquor shop

hint: It is the wheel you spin to make thread.
explanation: The **spinning wheel** (charkha) was used to make khadi, the hand-spun cloth, so it stood for the Gandhian ideal of **self-help**. It sat at the centre of the tricolour Swaraj flag (red, green and white) that Gandhiji had designed by 1921.
